Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- While all eyes seem to be on "Slumdog Millionaire" for the Oscars, one very courageous little girl will be focused on another India-based film at the ceremony. Pinki, like millions in developing countries, had to live with her deformity and suffer the social consequences. It's called "Smile Pinki," and it's up for an Oscar, too -- nominated for best short documentary, which it won on Sunday. The little girl watching it from inside the Oscar ceremony has traveled all the way to Los Angeles, California, from her small Indian village with her dad -- and it has been an incredible journey for Pinki Sonkar. "Smile Pinki" tells the story of her transformation from a sad outcast to a vibrant 8-year-old with plenty of spunk. Pinki was born with a cleft lip, and her impoverished family did not have the money for corrective surgery. Like millions of other children born with the lip deformity in developing countries, Pinki simply had to live with it and suffer the social consequences. Her father Rajendra Sonkar says: "She used to go to school and the kids would not befriend her. She would say, 'I don't want to go to school.'"  Watch how Pinki was transformed by the operation » . "Pinki was a depressed, sad, lonely, shy, young little girl, growing up on the periphery of the society in a little village," said Satish Kalra, director of Smile Train's South Asian region, after meeting with Pinki. The little girl's own family was ashamed of her, Kalra says. But all of that has changed. Pinki is now a real pistol, full of energy and confidence, and she has a fantastic smile too -- thanks to the Smile Train charity. Smile Train teaches doctors in their own countries to operate on cleft lips, a deformity afflicting up to four million children across the world. iReport: Share your Oscar predictions . Pinki just happened to be one of the chosen candidates for surgery and was also chosen to be the subject of the documentary. The film chronicles her transformation, following her from her village to the hospital and home again. "She has absolutely and totally changed," said Pinki's surgeon, Dr. Subodh Kumar. The film's director is Megan Mylan. She has won several awards but not an Oscar -- until now. For Pinki and her dad, being able to see the film's director win an Oscar would be a thrill. But they know they already have the greatest prize: Pinki's new smile. "I am so happy that my daughter's lips have been repaired," her dad Rajendra said with a smile, expressing hope that the movie will inspire people to help children whose families can't afford the surgery.

The movie, “Smile Pinki,” was also an Academy Award contender and was nominated for best short documentary — an award it won on Sunday.

Pinki Sonkar, who had come to Los Angeles, California, from a small village in India with her father, was inside the Oscar ceremony to watch the event. For her, the trip marked the latest chapter in an extraordinary journey.

“Smile Pinki” follows Pinki’s life-changing experience, showing how she went from being a sorrowful outsider to an energetic, spirited 8-year-old girl. She was born with a cleft lip, but her poor family could not pay for the surgery needed to repair it. Like millions of children in developing nations who are born with the same condition, Pinki was forced to live with the deformity and endure the painful social effects that came with it.

Her father, Rajendra Sonkar, said she once struggled at school because other children would not make friends with her. “She used to go to school and the kids would not befriend her. She would say, ‘I don’t want to go to school,’” he said.

After meeting Pinki, Satish Kalra, director of Smile Train’s South Asian region, described her as “a depressed, sad, lonely, shy, young little girl” who was growing up on the margins of society in a tiny village. Kalra also said that even Pinki’s own relatives felt ashamed of her.

But her life is very different now. With help from the charity Smile Train, Pinki has become lively, confident, and full of personality — and she now has a beautiful smile. Smile Train trains physicians in their own countries to perform cleft lip operations, addressing a condition that affects as many as four million children worldwide.

Pinki was selected to receive the surgery and was also chosen as the focus of the documentary. The film traces her journey from her village to the hospital and then back home, capturing the change in her life. Her surgeon, Dr. Subodh Kumar, said, “She has absolutely and totally changed.”

The documentary was directed by Megan Mylan, who had received several honors before but had not won an Oscar until this film. For Pinki and her father, witnessing Mylan receive the Academy Award would be exciting. Still, they understand that they have already received the most important reward: Pinki’s restored smile.

“I am so happy that my daughter’s lips have been repaired,” Rajendra said, smiling. He also expressed hope that the film would encourage others to assist children whose families cannot afford the operation.

**From a village in India to the Oscars: The story behind “Smile Pinki”**

**VARANASI, India** — Pinki Sonkar was a little girl from rural northern India whose cleft lip had shaped much of her early childhood — how others saw her, how she felt about herself and whether she felt welcome at school.

Then a simple surgery changed her life, and a short documentary about that transformation took her all the way to Hollywood.

Pinki became known around the world as the subject of **“Smile Pinki,”** the Oscar-winning documentary short directed by **Megan Mylan**. The film followed Pinki, a young girl from **Uttar Pradesh**, as she received free corrective surgery for a cleft lip through the international charity **Smile Train**.

For children born with cleft lips and palates, the condition can make eating and speaking difficult. In many communities, it can also bring stigma and isolation. In Pinki’s case, the documentary showed how her appearance affected her confidence and her place among other children.

Her operation was performed in Varanasi by surgeons working with Smile Train, including cleft surgeon **Dr. Subodh Kumar Singh**, whose work has helped thousands of children receive treatment. The surgery itself was relatively short, but its impact was life-changing.

Afterward, Pinki’s smile — and her future — looked different. The film captured her return to village life and school, showing how access to basic medical care can alter the course of a child’s childhood.

That story resonated far beyond India.

In 2009, **“Smile Pinki” won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Short Subject** at the 81st Academy Awards. Pinki traveled to Los Angeles for the ceremony, a journey that carried her from a small village in India to the red carpet at one of the world’s most watched entertainment events.

Her presence at the Oscars became a symbol of the film’s broader message: that millions of children with cleft conditions can be helped through surgery, but many never receive care because of poverty, distance from hospitals or lack of awareness.

For Pinki, the spotlight was unexpected. She was not an actress playing a role, but a child whose real medical journey had been documented on film. Her trip to the Academy Awards brought global attention not only to her story, but to the needs of children like her.

“Smile Pinki” remains one of the best-known films about cleft repair and the difference a single medical procedure can make. At its center is a young girl whose smile became a powerful reminder that access to health care can change a life.

counterfactuals.output:
In a small village in Uttar Pradesh, India, a little girl named Pinki Sonkar grew up carrying a burden she had never chosen.

Pinki was born with a cleft lip, a condition that left a visible opening in her upper lip and made everyday life harder than it should have been. In her village, where medical information was limited and poverty narrowed every possibility, her cleft was more than a health issue. It shaped how people saw her, how other children treated her, and how she saw herself.

She was teased. She often kept away from school. Like many children born with clefts in rural communities, Pinki lived with a condition that was treatable, but seemed out of reach because her family could not afford surgery.

Then help arrived through Smile Train, an international charity that supports free cleft surgery and comprehensive cleft care for children around the world. Smile Train works by partnering with local doctors and hospitals, helping build sustainable treatment programs in the communities where children live.

Through one of these programs, Pinki was brought to a hospital where surgeons could repair her cleft lip. The operation itself was not long, but its impact was life-changing.

After surgery, Pinki’s face began to heal — and so did something deeper. The little girl who had been hidden by shame and stigma slowly stepped into a new life. She could smile more freely. She could return to school. Her family saw doors open that had once seemed permanently closed.

Pinki’s story might have remained a quiet miracle in one Indian village. Instead, it reached the world.

Filmmaker Megan Mylan documented Pinki’s journey in the short film *Smile Pinki*. The documentary did not tell her story as a fairy tale, but as a deeply human portrait of poverty, medicine, family love, and the difference a simple surgery can make. It showed Pinki before and after the operation, as well as the efforts of medical workers and Smile Train-supported programs to find children who needed care.

In 2009, *Smile Pinki* won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Short Subject. Pinki, still a child, traveled to the Oscars — a journey almost unimaginable from the village where she had once been mocked for the way she looked.

Her presence on that global stage became a symbol of hope for thousands of children with clefts. It showed that a condition often surrounded by stigma could be treated. It reminded the world that behind every statistic is a child waiting to eat, speak, learn, laugh, and be accepted.

Pinki Sonkar’s transformation was not just about a repaired lip. It was about dignity restored. It was about a family discovering that their daughter’s future could be different. And it was about the power of organizations like Smile Train to connect medical skill with children who might otherwise never receive care.

From a village in India to the red carpet at the Oscars, Pinki’s smile became more than her own. It became a message: sometimes, a life can change with one surgery — and one child’s story can change how the world sees millions more.

*Entertainment/Health News — CNN-style feature*

When *Slumdog Millionaire* swept through Hollywood’s awards season, much of the world’s attention turned to India’s streets, dreams and improbable journeys. But on the same Oscar night, another Indian story — quieter, smaller and deeply personal — captured hearts: *Smile Pinki*, the Academy Award-winning documentary short about a little girl whose life changed after surgery repaired her cleft lip.

The film follows Pinki Sonkar, a young girl from a poor village in Uttar Pradesh, India, who was born with a cleft lip. Before surgery, Pinki faced teasing, isolation and difficulty attending school — challenges common for many children with untreated cleft conditions, particularly in rural areas with limited access to medical care.

Her journey took an extraordinary turn when she received free corrective surgery from Dr. Subodh Kumar Singh, a cleft surgeon in Varanasi. The procedure, relatively short by surgical standards, had life-altering consequences. Pinki’s repaired smile helped transform not only her appearance, but also her confidence and sense of belonging.

The documentary’s success carried Pinki far from her village — all the way to Los Angeles, where she attended the Academy Awards. Standing in the glow of Hollywood’s biggest night, Pinki became an unlikely symbol of what access to basic surgery can mean for a child’s future.

Her father, who had watched his daughter endure stigma and exclusion, also became part of the emotional arc of the story. For families like Pinki’s, the surgery represented more than medical treatment; it offered the possibility of school, friendships and a childhood less defined by shame.

The visibility of *Smile Pinki* helped draw attention to cleft lip and palate repair, a form of surgery that can dramatically improve eating, speech development, social acceptance and overall quality of life. Health advocates say the film showed global audiences that a repairable condition can become a lifelong burden when poverty blocks access to care.

As *Slumdog Millionaire* celebrated India’s cinematic presence on the world stage, *Smile Pinki* offered a different kind of triumph — one measured not in box-office success, but in a child’s ability to smile freely.

For Pinki, the trip to Los Angeles was a once-unimaginable adventure. But the true turning point came before the red carpet: in an operating room, with a surgeon who helped give her back something many take for granted — the chance to face the world with confidence.
